### surv-potassium-iodide

- Tags: none. Links: s:surv-fallout-warning, s:surv-dirty-bomb, p:anaphylaxis. Title changed from the plan's "what it does
  and does not do" to "Potassium iodide (KI): what it can and can't do" (search pins "no" to CPR; see rulings).
- No dose, no dose table, no age bands with amounts, no tablet strengths. CDC-KI's 24-hours-before / 4-hours-after timing,
  its "One dose of KI offers protection for 24 hours" and its breastfeeding advice are not used (D103, D102).
- doFirst 1: CDC-KI ("The best protection in a radiation emergency is always to get inside, stay inside, and stay tuned").
- doFirst 2: CDC-KI ("Leaving your shelter or home to seek KI could expose you to dangerous levels of radiation" / "and put you
  and your loved ones at greater risk.").
- doFirst 3: CDC-KI ("Do not take KI unless you are instructed by public health or emergency response officials or a
  healthcare provider.").
- doFirst 4: CDC-KI ("Do not use table salt or foods that contain iodine as a substitute for KI."; "They do not help prevent
  internal contamination, and eating large amounts could be harmful."; "Dietary supplements that contain iodine may not work
  to protect the thyroid and can hurt you.").
- What it does: CDC-KI ("Potassium iodide (KI) is a type of iodine that is not radioactive."; "The thyroid is a gland in the
  neck"; "there is no room to absorb the radioactive iodine."; "KI protects only the thyroid."; "KI does not protect other
  parts of the body."; "KI protects only against radioactive iodine and does not protect against other types of radioactive
  materials."; "KI is most effective if taken shortly before or right after internal contamination with radioactive
  iodine."; "KI may not give a person 100% thyroid protection from radioactive iodine."; "KI is not a treatment and cannot
  reverse damage already done to the thyroid."); FDA-KI ("It is not a general radioprotective agent.").
- After a nuclear explosion: CDC-KI section "KI will not help in a nuclear bomb emergency", every sentence ("Radiation from
  radioactive fallout is the biggest threat to your health after a nuclear detonation (explosion)."; "Fallout is made up of
  hundreds of types of radioactive materials."; "There is a relatively small amount of radioactive iodine in fallout compared
  to other types of radioactive materials" / "that can cause harm just by external exposure."; "KI would not protect you
  against the harmful health effects of any radioactive materials other than radioactive iodine."; "If you were in a situation
  to take in enough radioactive iodine for KI to be helpful, you would have been exposed to deadly levels of external
  radiation from fallout."), and "Risks of focusing on KI" ("You may think you are protected against radiation exposure when
  you are not.").
- After a dirty bomb: CDC-DB as in surv-dirty-bomb.
- When officials might call for it: CDC-KI ("Most radiation emergencies will involve other types of radioactive materials and
  not radioactive iodine alone."; "Radioactive iodine is most common in nuclear power plant incidents."); NYS-KI ("If there is
  an emergency, you will hear an announcement from your local or state health officials."; "Your local health department will
  tell you when you should start taking KI and they will also tell you when you can stop taking it."); FDA-KI ("After a
  radiological or nuclear event in the United States, local public health or emergency management officials" / "will tell
  the public if there is a need to take KI or other protective actions."). NYS-KI's plant-distance figure and its once-a-day
  instruction are not used (plant accidents deferred; D103). Scope line: spec 2 (no source needed).
- Who it is meant for: CDC-KI ("KI is only recommended for people under 40 and women who are pregnant or breastfeeding.";
  "This is because younger people's cells are still growing and increasing in number more quickly."; "This puts them at risk
  for developing thyroid cancer after breathing in radioactive iodine."; "Infants (under 1 month) have the highest risk of
  developing thyroid cancer from contamination with radioactive iodine."; "Adults over 40 years old have a much lower risk of
  developing thyroid cancer."; "They are also more likely to have health conditions, like problems with their thyroids," /
  "that increase the risk for harmful health effects from KI."; "Adults over 40 should only take KI when recommended by
  officials"). Number: 40 years and 1 month (CDC-KI); these are who-for limits, not doses.
- Who should not take it: CDC-KI ("People with certain medical conditions, including known iodine sensitivity, should not take
  KI" / "or should talk to a healthcare provider about whether they can safely take KI."); FDA-KI ("Persons with known iodine
  sensitivity should avoid KI, as should individuals with dermatitis herpetiformis" / "and hypocomplementemic vasculitis,
  extremely rare conditions associated with an increased risk" / "of iodine hypersensitivity."; "People with nodular thyroid
  with heart disease should not take KI."; "Individuals with multinodular goiter, Graves' disease, and autoimmune thyroiditis
  should be treated with caution" (FDA's "-- especially if dosing extends beyond a few days" is not used); "A seafood or
  shellfish allergy does not necessarily mean that you are allergic or hypersensitive to iodine."; "If you are not sure if you
  should take KI, consult your health care professional.").
- Risks: CDC-KI ("Gastro-intestinal (stomach) upset, rashes, and inflammation of the salivary glands."; "Allergic reaction.";
  "Severe illness or death in people who take more KI than recommended."; "More than a single dose may lead to later problems
  with normal development."; "The development of hypothyroidism in infants less than one month old who receive more than one
  dose of KI."); FDA-KI ("Taking a higher dose of KI, or taking KI more often than recommended, does not offer more protection"
  / "and can cause severe illness or death."; "Severe shortness of breath requires immediate medical attention."). Link
  p:anaphylaxis for a severe allergic reaction (not restated).
- What is not a substitute: CDC-KI (salt, iodine foods, supplements as in doFirst 4; "Only use KI products that have been
  approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)."); FEMA-PG3 p. 129 ("If social media posts encouraged people to drink
  iodine to protect themselves from radiation, what would you do?"; "How would you confront this rumor?"). FDA-KI does not
  address substitutes.
- If you keep KI: FDA-KI ("KI is available without a prescription."); CDC-KI ("KI should be used only as directed."; FDA-approved
  only). "Keeping KI is never a reason to go outside, delay getting inside, or leave shelter" rests on CDC-KI's risks of
  focusing on KI (leaving shelter to seek KI) and its reminder; "delay getting inside" is the app's reading of the same.

## Food pack batch A: food when the power goes out, is it still good, cook without power, food poisoning and botulism (2026-11-19)

Files (all draft): src/survival/surv-food-power-out.json (hub), surv-food-still-good.json, surv-food-cooking-no-power.json,
surv-food-poisoning.json. tests/test_build.py topic count 48 to 52. Gates and the indoor-cooking finding: docs/v7.5-rulings.md.
Every source below was found by built-in web search and opened by built-in web fetch on 2026-11-19; the title (and date where
printed) was checked after each fetch. Fetches return quotes capped at about 125 characters, so long sentences were read as
consecutive pieces, and the FoodSafety.gov charts were read in two fetches (fridge, then freezer) as row-by-row lists. No
Firecrawl, no Bright Data. No URL was constructed: each was returned by a search, or named in a page that was fetched
(FoodSafety.gov's chart URL was named by the HHS syndication page).

Source keys:
- CDC-KFS: CDC, Keep Food Safe After a Disaster or Emergency, last reviewed and updated November 24, 2025. https://www.cdc.gov/food-safety/foods/keep-food-safe-after-emergency.html
- CDC-PO: CDC, What to Do to Protect Yourself During a Power Outage, reviewed August 26, 2026. https://www.cdc.gov/natural-disasters/response/what-to-do-protect-yourself-during-a-power-outage.html
- CDC-PREV: CDC, Preventing Food Poisoning, last reviewed and updated November 24, 2025. https://cdc.gov/food-safety/prevention
- CDC-SYM: CDC, Food Poisoning Symptoms, dated November 24, 2025. https://www.cdc.gov/food-safety/signs-symptoms/index.html
- CDC-BOT: CDC, Symptoms of Botulism, page dated April 1, 2024. https://cdc.gov/botulism/signs-symptoms
- CDC-HC: CDC, Home-Canned Foods (botulism prevention), page dated April 25, 2024 (last published December 2, 2025). https://cdc.gov/botulism/prevention/home-canned-foods.html (opened twice)
- FSG-3: FoodSafety.gov (HHS), Three Ways to Keep Food Safe When You Lose Power, published October 8, 2020, modified September 21, 2023. https://www.foodsafety.gov/blog/three-ways-keep-food-safe-when-you-lose-power
- FSG-CH: FoodSafety.gov, Food Safety During Power Outage (the two charts), last reviewed August 8, 2024. https://www.foodsafety.gov/food-safety-charts/food-safety-during-power-outage (opened three times: summary, fridge chart, freezer chart)
- FSG-4: FoodSafety.gov, 4 Steps to Food Safety, last reviewed September 18, 2023. https://www.foodsafety.gov/keep-food-safe/4-steps-to-food-safety
- HHS-SYN: HHS Digital Media syndication page "Food Safety and Power Outages: When to Save and When to Throw Out". https://digitalmedia.hhs.gov/storefront/showContent/105 (held no chart; named FSG-CH's URL; not cited)
- FSIS-EM: USDA FSIS, Keeping Food Safe During an Emergency (English page at the /es/ node address; no date printed). https://www.fsis.usda.gov/es/node/3347 (opened three times)
- FSIS-TEMP: USDA FSIS, Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart, last updated April 14, 2025. https://www.fsis.usda.gov/es/node/3293
- FSIS-MOLD: USDA FSIS, Molds on Food: Are They Dangerous? (English; no date printed). https://www.fsis.usda.gov/es/node/3303
- NYS-FF: New York State Department of Health, The Fridge and Freezer: When the Power is Out, revised October 2023. https://healthweb-back.health.ny.gov/environmental/emergency/flood/fridge_freezer_no_power.htm (opened twice)
- NYS-BOT: New York State Department of Health, Botulism Fact Sheet, revised December 2025. https://healthweb-back.health.ny.gov/diseases/communicable/botulism/fact_sheet.htm (opened twice)

- NYS-DPS: New York State Department of Public Service, Electric and Natural Gas Safety Tips (05/22rv). https://dps.ny.gov/system/files/documents/2023/12/electric-and-natural-gas-safety-tips.pdf (indoor-cooking finding only; not cited in a topic)
- READY-F: Ready.gov, Food / Suggested Food Supplies (no date in the fetch result). https://ready.gov/food (opened twice)
- EPA-PO: EPA, Power Outages and Indoor Air Quality (IAQ), last updated February 18, 2026. https://epa.gov/emergencies-iaq/power-outages-and-indoor-air-quality-iaq and https://www.epa.gov/node/264249 (same page; both opened)
- EPA-CP: EPA, Sources of Combustion Products, last updated November 10, 2026. https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq/sources-combustion-products-introduction-indoor-air-quality

- MA-GRILL: Massachusetts Department of Fire Services, Grilling Safety (no date printed). https://mass.gov/info-details/grilling-safety
- NYDCP-GR: New York State Department of State, Division of Consumer Protection, Consumer Alert on gas and charcoal grills, May 14, 2024. https://dos.ny.gov/news/consumer-alert-ny-department-states-division-consumer-protection-provides-safety-tips-follow (opened twice)
- NCHFP-SP: National Center for Home Food Preservation, Identifying and Handling Spoiled Canned Food (no date; adapted from a USDA bulletin revised 2015). https://nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-information/identifying-and-handling-spoiled-canned-food/

- UGA-EFS: University of Georgia Extension, Preparing an Emergency Food Supply, Long Term Food Storage (reviewed 2017). https://www.fcs.uga.edu/extension/preparing-an-emergency-food-supply-long-term-food-storage (Tool gate only)

(https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/foodborne-illness-and-disease/illnesses-and-pathogens/botulism, client error); FEMA,
Food and Water in an Emergency (fema.gov PDF client error; carbon.utah.gov copy robots-blocked; UNT archive returned only its
viewer); ready.gov/power-outages (client error); Purdue Extension dry ice note (.docx returned as binary data); MedlinePlus
Botulism (nlm.nih.gov redirected to medlineplus.gov; the follow-up fetch was refused by the session's permission prompt).

Conversions (app's own): 0°F = -18°C; 1 inch = 2.5 cm; 3 feet = 1 m and 10 feet = 3 m (as the checked heat topics write
them); 1,000 feet = 300 m; 8 quarts = 7.6 L. Celsius in the temperature table is USDA's own (62.8, 71.1, 73.9); 40°F (4°C),
50°F (10°C), 90°F (32°C) and 140°F (60°C) are FoodSafety.gov's own.

### surv-food-power-out (hub; leads the Food category)

- Tags: none. Links: s:surv-food-still-good (twice), s:surv-generators, s:surv-food-cooking-no-power, s:surv-food-poisoning,
  s:surv-fallout-water-and-food, s:surv-field-dressing-game, s:surv-food-and-wild-plants, s:surv-traps-and-fishing. Every label
  equals its target's title. Links left for later tasks: docs/v7.5-rulings.md. The hub-lead entry in src/survival.js is Task 8's.
- Owner of: fridge and freezer hold times (spec 7).
- doFirst 1 / table "How long it stays cold": CDC-KFS ("If the doors stay closed, food will stay safe up to: 4 hours in a
  refrigerator, 48 hours in a full freezer," / "24 hours in a half-full freezer."); CDC-PO ("A full freezer will keep food safe
  for 48 hours (24 hours if half-full) without power if you don't open the door."; "Your refrigerator will keep food safe for up
  to 4 hours without power if you don't open the door."); FSG-3 ("A refrigerator will keep food cold for about 4 hours if the
  door is kept closed."; "A full freezer will hold its temperature for about 48 hours, or 24 hours if it is half-full, if you
  don't open the door."); FSIS-EM ("The refrigerator will keep food safely cold for about 4 hours if it is unopened."; "A full
  freezer will hold the temperature for approximately 48 hours (24 hours if it is half full)" / "if the door remains closed.");
  NYS-FF ("Food in the refrigerator will remain cold for about 4 hours if the door stays shut."; "A fully-filled freezer will
  stay at freezing temperature for about two days if the door stays shut."; "A half-full freezer will stay cold for about one
  day."). All agree. "About" is kept (FSG-3, FSIS-EM, NYS-FF).
- doFirst 2: NYS-FF ("Eat the most perishable items first, such as leftovers, meat, poultry, and foods containing milk," /
  "cream, sour cream, or soft cheese."). NYC-EM says "Use the perishable food in the refrigerator and freezer first." (not
  cited). FEMA's fridge-then-freezer-then-pantry order could not be opened (FEMA-477 failed) and is not used.
- doFirst 3 / "Keep it cold longer" 3: CDC-KFS ("If the power has been out for 4 hours, and a cooler and ice are available, put
  refrigerated perishable foods in the cooler."; "To keep them at 40°F or below, add ice or a cold source like frozen gel
  packs.").
- doFirst 4 / "Not outside, even in winter": NYS-FF ("Do not put your food outside to keep it cold, even in the winter."; "This
  is not a good idea because temperatures cold enough for refrigerated food are too warm for frozen food."; "And, even if it is
  very cold outside, the sun could warm the food to a temperature that would allow bacteria to grow."; "Also, animals could get
  into your food and contaminate it."); FSIS-EM ("No, frozen food can thaw if it is exposed to the sun's rays even when the
  temperature is very cold."; "The outside temperature could vary hour by hour and the temperature outside will not protect
  refrigerated and frozen food."; "Animals may harbor bacteria or disease; never consume food that has come in contact with an
  animal."; "Rather than putting the food outside, consider taking advantage of the cold temperatures by making ice."). The
  question FSIS-EM answers is not printed in the fetch; its answer is about putting food outside in cold weather.
- doFirst 5: links Is it still good? (the throw-out owner); CDC-KFS ("Never taste food to know if it is safe to eat.").
- "How long it stays cold" list: NYS-FF ("Don't open the doors any more than is needed to quickly check the temperature and
  get your food."; "Group items so they form an “igloo” to protect each other."; "Keep meats together on one side of the
  freezer or on a tray so that if they begin thawing," / "their juices won't get on other food."; "Foods with a high water
  content, such as meat or fruit, will stay frozen longer than food with a low" / "water content, such as bread."); FSIS-EM
  ("When your freezer is not full, keep items close together—this helps the food stay cold longer.").
- "Keep it cold longer": NYS-FF ("Put ice or frozen water containers in fridge or freezer to keep your food cold,"; "If you
  think power will be out for several days, purchase dry ice or block ice"); CDC-KFS ("Buy dry ice or block ice to keep food
  cold in the refrigerator if you think the power could be out for a long time."); FSIS-EM ("Fill buckets, empty milk cartons or
  cans with water and leave them outside to freeze."; "Then put the homemade ice in your refrigerator, freezer, or coolers.").
  "In freezing weather" is the app's lead-in to FSIS's cold-temperature answer. Dry ice left out (rulings 5; D127).
- "Thermometers": CDC-KFS ("Keep appliance thermometers in your refrigerator and freezer."; "The refrigerator should be at 40°F
  or below."; "The freezer should be at 0°F or below."); NYS-FF ("use an appliance thermometer in fridge and freezer when the
  power is out."); FSIS-EM ("If you're not sure a particular food is cold enough, take its temperature with a food
  thermometer.").
- "After 4 hours, or when the power comes back": FSG-3 ("After the power outage, check each food item separately."); CDC-KFS
  ("When in doubt, throw it out.").
- "A generator for the fridge or freezer": Generators' Do first 1, quoted word for word. No generator rule restated.
- "Get ready before it happens": CDC-KFS ("Keep appliance thermometers..."; "Freeze containers of water and gel packs to help
  keep food at 40°F or below."; "Have a cooler and frozen gel packs ready in case you have to remove food from the refrigerator
  to keep it cold."); FSIS-EM ("by having items on hand that don't require refrigeration and can be eaten cold or heated on the
  outdoor grill."; "Be sure to keep a hand-held can opener for an emergency.").
- Looked for and not found: how long a chest freezer holds compared with an upright (no source distinguishes them; the
  full/half-full times are used for both); any source allowing a cold room, porch, garage or snow as a fridge (NYS-FF and
  FSIS-EM both say no).

  the cans or retort pouches with water that is safe for drinking, if available,"; boil 2 minutes or the 1-tablespoon solution 15
  minutes; "Air-dry cans or retort pouches for a minimum of 1 hour before opening or storing."; re-label "including the expiration
  date (if available), with a marker."; use as soon as possible. The topic merges CDC's and USDA's steps in that order (CDC brushes

  countertops with soap and water, using hot water if available."; "Rinse and then sanitize them by applying a solution of 1

## Food pack batch B: how much food to store, store food so it lasts, when food is short, Pantry checklist (2026-11-19)

Files (all draft): src/survival/surv-food-how-much.json, surv-food-storage.json, surv-food-when-short.json,
src/checklists/pantry.json. tests/test_build.py topic count 52 to 55. Rulings: docs/v7.5-rulings.md "Batch B"; questions D130 to
D139. Every source below was found by built-in web search and opened by built-in web fetch on 2026-11-19; the title (and date where
printed) was checked after each fetch. Fetches return quotes capped at about 125 characters, so long sentences were read as
consecutive pieces (marked " / "). No Firecrawl, no Bright Data. No URL was constructed: each was returned by a search.

Source keys:
- READY-F: Ready.gov (FEMA), Food, "Suggested Emergency Food Supplies", Last Updated 03/30/2022. https://www.ready.gov/food (opened twice)
- READY-KIT: Ready.gov (FEMA), Build A Kit, "Emergency Supply List" and "Maintaining Your Kit" (no date in the fetch result). https://www.ready.gov/kit
- ARC-KIT: American Red Cross, "What Do You Need In a Survival Kit" (heading "Survival Kit Supplies"; no date, footer © 2026). https://redcross.org/get-help/how-to-prepare-for-emergencies/survival-kit-supplies.html
- FW: FEMA in cooperation with the American Red Cross and USDA, Food and Water in an Emergency (no date or number printed; county-hosted copy). https://henrycounty.in.gov/DocumentCenter/View/295/Food-and-Water-in-an-Emergency-PDF (opened three times). The same lines were checked in FW-1994.
- FW-1994: the same booklet as "FEMA Triangle: Food and Water in an Emergency", footer ARC 5055 / FEMA L-210, November 1994, "Reprinted by permission of the American Red Cross (1997)". https://qsl.net/n0njy/foodwtr.html (used to date the booklet: "two weeks", "rationed safely, except for children and pregnant women", "half their usual food intake", salty foods, storage tips and the shelf-life lists are in it). - UGA-ST: University of Georgia Extension (Elizabeth Andress, Ph.D., and Judy Harrison, Ph.D.), Preparing an Emergency Food Supply, Short Term Food Storage, reviewed March 2020. https://www.fcs.uga.edu/extension/preparing-an-emergency-food-supply-short-term-food-storage
- UGA-EFS: University of Georgia Extension (Judy Harrison, Ph.D., and Elizabeth Andress, Ph.D.), Preparing an Emergency Food Supply, Long Term Food Storage, reviewed 2017. https://www.fcs.uga.edu/extension/preparing-an-emergency-food-supply-long-term-food-storage (re-opened twice for this batch)

- FSIS-DATE: USDA FSIS, Food Product Dating (English; no date). https://www.fsis.usda.gov/es/node/3294

emergency supply of shelf-stable food for one person" (foodsmartcolorado.colostate.edu redirected to a general Colorado State page,
not followed). Nothing from these is in a topic.

Looked for and not found: a current federal, New York State or extension statement of food per person per day or per child for an
emergency store (Ready.gov, Red Cross, DHSES, NYS-KIT, ILL-EFS, UGA-ST, UMN-2W, OSU-SB, Cornell Warren County: days only; UMN-2W's
menu is "designed for two people" with recipes for "four to six adults", no per-person amount); signs that someone is not getting

definitions and news, none used); how a group should share food; any source besides FW on rationing food; any source saying a
nursing mother or a sick person may eat less.

Conversions (app's own): 85°F = 29°C; 100°F = 38°C; 50°F and 70°F = 10°C and 21°C (as Protect an unheated house writes them);
130°F = 54°C; 0°F = -18°C; 40°F = 4°C (as the checked topics write it). Pounds to kilograms at 0.4536 kg per lb, rounded: 240 lb =
109 kg, 120 lb = 54 kg, 75 lb = 34 kg, 42 lb = 19 kg, 40 lb = 18 kg, 25 lb = 11.3 kg, 20 lb = 9.1 kg, 17 lb = 7.7 kg, 5 lb = 2.3 kg,
4 lb = 1.8 kg, 1 lb = 0.45 kg, 1/2 lb = 0.23 kg; 1/2 gal = 1.9 L.

  nuts; Vitamin C. "May be stored indefinitely" list not used (D137). OSU-SB "Dried beans stored for more than three years may not
  rehydrate."; "Freeze-dried foods may boast a 20- to 30-year storage life, but don’t ensure quality." "When opened, they will spoil

- Agreement with Water and food after fallout "Babies": that section governs after fallout and is linked ("After fallout, breastfeeding
  and formula have their own rules"). Both say ready-to-feed first and bottled water for powdered formula (CDC). This topic's general
  order (bottled, then boiled and cooled, then treated only if neither: CDC-FYC) does not apply after fallout, where boiling and
  bleach do not remove fallout; the link sentence sends readers there. D115 (stored water for formula after fallout) is unchanged.
- doFirst 1: CDC-BFE ("In emergencies, breastfeeding is the safest way to feed your baby."); CDC-IFQ ("You can continue to breastfeed
  and express breast milk even if you are feeling physical and emotional stress.").
- doFirst 2 / Mixing step 3: CDC-PIF ("ready-to-feed (RTF) infant formula is the safest option."; "RTF infant formula is a sterile,
  liquid infant formula that is ready to feed without adding water."; "Use bottled water to prepare powdered formula until local
  authorities say the tap water is safe to drink."; "If bottled water is not available, learn how to make water safe by boiling or
  disinfecting."); CDC-FYC ("If bottled water is not available, boil water for 1 minute and let it cool before mixing with formula.";
  "Only use treated water to prepare formula if bottled or boiled water is unavailable."). READY-F ("If you must mix infant formula use
  bottled water or boiled water as a last resort.") does not mention treated water (D140).
- doFirst 3 / warn: CDC-PIF ("Always use the exact amount of water and formula listed on the instructions of the infant formula
  container."; "Adding too much or too little formula can make your baby sick."; "Do not make or feed your baby homemade infant
  formula."; "Feeding homemade infant formula can lead to serious health problems."). "Never water formula down to make it last" is the
  app's plain restatement of "too much or too little" (no separate source sentence; FDA-HIF was summarised as saying too much water
  will "not provide enough nutrition", not quoted verbatim, and is not cited for it).
- doFirst 4 / Mixing list 1: CDC-PIF ("During power outages, you may not have access to a working refrigerator."; "In this case,
  prepare fresh formula for every feeding."; "Throw out any formula that's left over after feeding your baby."; "Do not refrigerate it
  to save for later."; "If you are not going to use the prepared formula within 2 hours, immediately store it in the refrigerator" /
  "and use within 24 hours."); FDA-HIF ("If it is not used immediately, store the bottle in the refrigerator and use it within 24
  hours.").
- doFirst 5 / "Before 12 months": CDC-AVL ("Do not give your child honey before 12 months."; "Do not add honey to your baby's food,
  water, infant formula, or pacifier."; cow's milk "may put them at risk for intestinal bleeding", "too many proteins and minerals for
  your baby's kidneys to handle easily", "does not have the right amount of nutrients your baby needs"; "Children younger than 12 months
  should not drink any fruit or vegetable juice."); CDC-MILK ("You can introduce your child to whole cow's milk at 12 months old (but not
  before)."; "Fortified dairy alternatives can include beverages made from plants, such as soy, oat, rice, coconut, cashew, and almond.";
  "These milk alternatives should not be given before your child is 12 months old."). Honey warn: Food poisoning and botulism's warn,
  word for word (New York State Department of Health).
- doFirst 6 / choking sections: see below.
- Breastfeeding list: CDC-BFE ("Helps protect your baby from germs that can cause colds, ear infections, diarrhea, and vomiting.";
  "Keeps your baby hydrated."; "If your baby is less than 6 months old, they do not need to drink water or any other liquids, even in hot
  weather."; "If you think you have less breast milk than normal, breastfeed more often to increase your breast milk supply."; "If you
  are worried that your baby is not breastfeeding well, talk to a health care provider right away."); CDC-FYC ("during an emergency you

  milk by hand."; "If there is a power outage, you may not be able to use your electric breast pump."; "During and after a disaster,
  stay with your child."; "Staying together makes it much easier to continue breastfeeding."); CDC-IFQ ("You can and should continue
  breastfeeding while sick with certain illnesses such as the flu, COVID-19, or diarrhea" / "or if you have a breast infection such as
  mastitis."; "Be sure to wash your hands with soap and safe water or use a hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol" / "to help prevent
  spreading germs."; relactation: "Relactation is when you start breastfeeding again after having stopped for some time (weeks or

  (Ready.gov)"), linked, no amount.
- Stored breast milk: CDC-BMS ("At room temperature (77°F or colder) for up to 4 hours."; "Breast milk can be stored in an insulated
  cooler with frozen ice packs for up to 24 hours when traveling."; "Never refreeze breast milk after it has thawed."; "Once breast milk
  is brought to room temperature or warmed, use it within 2 hours."; "If your baby did not finish the bottle, use the leftover milk
  within 2 hours."; "After 2 hours, leftover breast milk should be discarded."; "Breast milk does not need to be warmed."; "Never thaw
  or heat breast milk in a microwave."; "Do not heat breast milk directly on the stove or in the microwave."); CDC-IFQ ("Frozen breast
  milk that has started to thaw but still contains ice crystals can be refrozen."; "If your breast milk has completely thawed but still

  "completely thawed" (never refreeze) and "still has ice crystals" (can be refrozen). The cooler time is labelled "CDC gives this for

  links). Thawed milk with no fridge: D144.
- Formula, which kind: CDC-PIF ("Powdered infant formula is not sterile."; "If your baby is less than 2 months old, was born

  younger than 3 months (D145).
- Mixing steps: CDC-PIF step 1 ("Clean your preparation surface."; "Wash your hands with soap and water."; "If water is not available

- Cleaning: CDC-CLN, all of it in its order ("Clean all items after every use"; the item list; "Use water that has not been used for

  5 minutes." "Remove items carefully." "Air dry sanitized items." "Do NOT rinse sanitized items."). Method 2 ("Add 1 teaspoon of bleach
  per 1/2 gallon or 8 cups of water." "Soak for 2 minutes." not rinsed) is not given (D141). FDA-HIF allows air drying "on a paper towel
  or clean dish towel"; CDC-CLN (emergencies) says never a dish towel: CDC used (more cautious). Floodwater items agree with Is it still
  good? ("Wooden cutting boards, baby bottle nipples and pacifiers that touched flood water").
- From 12 months: CDC-MILK ("Children can drink unflavored, unsweetened whole cow's milk."; "Choose one that is unflavored and

  "Do not give your child raw or unpasteurized milk." and "These harmful bacteria and germs can make your child very sick and can be
  life-threatening."); CDC-AVL (unpasteurized juice, milk, yogurt, cheeses; "Children younger than 24 months should not have added
  sugars."; caffeinated drinks before 24 months; "Juice after 12 months is unnecessary."; "The American Academy of Pediatrics

  serving fish caught by family and friends, check for fish and shellfish advisories."). CDC-MILK's "about 2 servings of dairy daily"
  for 12 through 23 months is a feeding amount and is not given (spec 10, call 9: the app adds no feeding amounts it does not need;
  it is sourced, but no serving size was given in the fetch). Children need more water: How much water you need, linked.

- Choking: warn USDA-CH ("Children under the age of 4 are at a high risk of choking while eating."), AAP-CH ("Keep high-risk foods from
  children until 4 years of age or older, depending on each child's development and maturity level."). Food list merged from CDC-CH
  (every item kept: corn kernels, uncut cherry or grape tomatoes, hard raw vegetables or fruit, whole pieces of canned fruit, uncut
  grapes, berries, cherries or melon balls, uncooked dried vegetables or fruit such as raisins, whole or chopped nuts and seeds, chunks
  or spoonfuls of nut and seed butters, tough or large chunks of meat, hot dogs, meat sticks or sausages, large chunks of cheese

  carrot sticks; raw apple chunks; popcorn; thick chunks of nut butter, "be sure to spread thinly instead"; marshmallows; meat sticks
  or sausages; chunks of meat; chunks of cheese or string cheese) and USDA-CH (adds dried fruit, hard pretzels and pretzel chips, ice
  cubes, cough drops, lollipops; "avoid serving foods that are as wide around as a nickel," / "which is about the size of a young
  child's throat."). "Gum drops" is under "gummy candy". Preparation: USDA-CH verbatim tips ("Cook or steam hard food, like carrots,
  until it is soft enough to pierce with a fork."; "Remove seeds, pits, and tough skins/peels from fruits and vegetables."; "Finely chop
  foods into thin slices, strips, or small pieces (no larger than ½ inch), or grate, mash, or puree foods."; "Remove all bones from
  fish, chicken, and meat before cooking or serving."; "Grind up tough meats and poultry."; "Grate or thinly slice cheese before
  serving."; "Slice these items in half lengthwise." then "slice into smaller pieces (no larger than ½ inch)"; "Cut tube-shaped foods,
  such as baby carrots, string cheese, hot dogs, etc., into short strips rather than round pieces."); AAP-CH ("Cut food for infants and
  young children into pieces no larger than one-half inch"); CDC-SOL ("Cut cylindrical foods like hot dogs, sausage, and string cheese
  into short thin strips."). Eating: CDC-CH ("Have your child sit up while eating (no lying down, crawling, or walking)."; "Have your
  child sit in a high chair or other safe place."; "Avoid letting your child eat in the car or stroller."; "Keep mealtimes calm.";
  "Avoid distractions, disruptions, and rushing when eating."; "Watch your child at all times while they are eating."); AAP-CH ("Never
  let them run, walk, play or lie down with food in their mouths."; "Many choking incidents happen when older brothers or sisters give
  dangerous foods, toys or small objects to a younger child."); USDA-CH ("Sit and eat with children at meals and snacks."; "Remind
  children to take small bites of food and swallow between bites."; "Reminding children to swallow their food before talking or
  laughing."; "When serving infants, do not prop the bottle up on a pillow or other item for the baby to feed him or herself.";
  "Making sure children are sitting upright while eating."; "All children should avoid playing games with food"). Choking care: the
  two protocols by link; their age split (infant under about 1 year) is the protocols' own.
- A sick baby or child: Dehydration protocol's "Babies: keep breastfeeding (WHO)." quoted in short form; Stay warm when the heat is out
  linked for a baby in a cold house.
- When formula runs out: no source opened says what to feed a baby under 12 months when there is no formula and no breast milk. D143.
  READY-F: "Food for infants" and "Use ready-to-feed formula." for keeping it in supplies.
- Looked for and not found: CDC or FDA guidance on what to feed an infant when formula runs out and nobody can breastfeed (CDC-IFQ and
  CDC-FYC are silent; FDA-DD only forbids homemade formula); how long opened ready-to-feed formula keeps without a fridge (FDA-HIF: the
  label); breastfeeding guidance for the mother's own food in a shortage (left to When food is short, a later page); any CDC, AAP or
  USDA figure for how much a child should eat (none is given; spec 10 call 9).

  touch ready-to-eat food with bare hands; use utensils (University of Minnesota Extension)."; "Wash dishes and food surfaces, then
  sanitize them with bleach (see Clean and disinfect)."); Clean and disinfect ("Use disposable plates, cups and cutlery if you have
  them (CDC)."; "Throw away food and food packaging within 25 feet (7.6 m) of the vomit or stool (University of Minnesota Extension).").
- doFirst 1 / Hands list: FSG-4 ("Before, during, and after preparing food"; "After handling raw meat, poultry, seafood, or their

  is sick"); "before feeding children" is CDC's as Washing hands with little water gives it; "the cleanest water you have" is that

- doFirst 3 / Raw and cooked apart: FSG-4 ("Use one cutting board for fresh produce or other foods that won't be cooked before they're

### surv-food-preserving

- Title: "Preserving food" (spec proposal "Preserve food without a freezer"; changed because "freezer" as a title word put this page

  (twice), s:surv-food-cooking-no-power (twice), s:surv-food-poisoning.
- No canning procedure of any kind (spec 10, call 3): no processing time, pressure, jar, headspace or recipe. The 240 to 250°F figure

  "pressure canner" (no PSIG given).
- Quoted word for word from checked topics: Is it still good? ("Don't eat home-canned food if you don't know whether safe canning
  guidelines were followed (CDC)."; "You cannot see, smell or taste the toxin that causes botulism, and even a small taste of food that
  has it can be deadly (CDC)."; its freezer rule "once the freezer is above 40°F (4°C), throw out thawed food (New York State
  Department of Health, CDC). Food that still has ice crystals or is at 40°F (4°C) or below can be refrozen or cooked (CDC,
  FoodSafety.gov)."); Food when the power goes out ("Don't put your food outside to keep it cold, even in the winter (New York State
  Department of Health)."). Boiling home-canned food and disposal are linked, not restated.
- doFirst 2 / Canning list: CDC-HC ("Pressure canning is the only recommended method for canning low-acid foods."; "Do not use a
  boiling water canner for low-acid foods because it will not protect against botulism."; "Do not use an electric, multi-cooker
  appliance, even if it has a "canning" or "steam canning" button on the front panel."; "Home-canned vegetables, which are low-acid
  foods, are the most common cause of botulism outbreaks in the United States."; "These foods include all fresh vegetables, figs,
  meats, poultry, fish, seafood, and some tomatoes."; "These instructions are in the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning."; "Use only
  recipes and cookbooks that follow the steps in the USDA guide."; "Land-grant colleges often provide information on growing and
  preserving food."; NCHFP "Get information for safely canning, preserving, pickling, fermenting, freezing, drying, curing and smoking,"
  / "and storing food."). "Don't try canning for the first time now" is labelled as the app's caution (spec 10 call 3).
- Canning list 3 and 4: NCHFP-ESC ("may produce a deadly toxin within 3 to 4 days of growth in an environment consisting of:" "a
  moist, low-acid food," "a temperature between 40° and 120°F," and "less than 2 percent oxygen"; "Botulinum spores are very hard to
  destroy at boiling-water temperatures;"; "Therefore, all low-acid foods should be sterilized at temperatures of 240° to 250°F," /
  "attainable with pressure canners operated at 10 to 15 PSIG.").
- doFirst 4 / Drying: NCHFP-SUN ("Vegetables (with the exception of vine dried beans) and meats are not recommended for out-of-doors
  drying."; "Vegetables are low in sugar and acid."; "Meats are high in protein, making them ideal for microbial growth when heat and
  humidity cannot be controlled."; "It is best to dry meats and vegetables indoors using controlled conditions of an oven or food
  dehydrator."; "To dry fruits out-of-doors hot, dry, breezy days are best."; "A minimum temperature of 85ºF is needed with higher
  temperatures being better."; "It takes several days to dry foods out-of-doors."; "A humidity below 60 percent is best."; "Fruits
  dried out-of-doors must be covered or brought under shelter at night."). The vine-dried beans exception is not given (no method for
  it was opened). PSU-DRY ("While sun drying works in dry climates, the high humidity in Pennsylvania makes this method impractical
  here."; oven "140 (60°C) to 150°F (65°C)"; dehydrator "145°F (62°C)" then "135 (57°C) to 140°F (60°C)"; and, as the first fetch summarised
  it (not quoted, not used), pasteurizing dried fruit in a freezer or an oven). None of these figures is in the topic. Why no drying method: v7.5-rulings.md Batch C ruling 2.
- Salting and curing / Smoking: NCHFP-CSS section 6 ("store, age, cure, or otherwise preserve meats in a refrigerator below 40°F.";
  "Curing should be carried out at a temperature between 35°F and 40°F."; "Mistakenly using sodium nitrite instead of NaCl in typical
  curing recipes can lead to a lethal dose"; "Smoke itself, without proper cooking, is not an effective food preservative (Hilderbrand
  1999)."; "Store Cured/Smoked Poultry up to two weeks in the refrigerator or up to one year in the freezer"; "Store lightly cured fish

  perishable product that rarely keeps better than the raw fish."). Section 5 (botulism thrives in moist foods low in salt; 65% of
  botulism cases from inadequate home processing) read and not used. NCHFP-CSS also says properly prepared dry cured hams are safe at

- Cold storage: links only; root cellars deferred (spec 10 call 5).

### food-fridge-freezer (surv-food-power-out, "How long it stays cold", after the table and its source paragraph)

- Title "Keep the fridge and freezer doors shut": Do first 1, "Keep the fridge and freezer doors shut."
- Three bands, in the table's order, split by dashed dividers. Each band: the appliance, "keeps food cold for", the hold time,
  "with the door shut", so no number stands without its condition. From the table (head "With the door shut" / "Keeps food
  cold for"; rows "Fridge | About 4 hours", "Full freezer | About 48 hours", "Half-full freezer | About 24 hours") and Do first
  1, "With the doors shut, a fridge keeps food cold for about 4 hours, a full freezer about 48 hours and a half-full freezer
  about 24 hours (CDC, FoodSafety.gov, USDA)."
- Fridge: a closed fridge seen from the front, handle on the door (door shut).
- Full freezer / Half-full freezer: a chest freezer seen from the front with its front wall cut away so the load shows; the
  lid is drawn shut on the body. Full: packed nearly to the lid. Half-full: food to about half the height, packed side by side
  ("When the freezer is not full, keep items close together", USDA, in the list below; no label drawn for it).
- "Before you eat, cook or refreeze anything, check it in Is it still good?": Do first 5, first sentence. It keeps the hold
  times from reading as a promise that food is fine.
- Not drawn: the thermometer and 40°F/0°F ("Check the temperature" is another section; temperatures beside the hours would
  give a tired reader two kinds of number to mix up), opening the doors to check, ice, coolers, not outside, generators,
  NYSDOH's "about two days / about one day".
- Caption: "Keep the fridge and freezer doors shut. With the doors shut, a fridge keeps food cold for about 4 hours, a full
  freezer about 48 hours and a half-full freezer about 24 hours (CDC, FoodSafety.gov, USDA). Before you eat, cook or refreeze
  anything, check it in Is it still good?" Do first 1 and the first sentence of Do first 5, word for word.

  treatments". Wash: MSU-DAN "Wash all leaves, flowers, and roots"; UVM-DAN "rinse them well". (Both are said of dandelion; the page

  anything with brambles except harvesting." PSU-RB: wild in disturbed areas (roadsides, logged woods, clearings, abandoned fields,
  fencerows; roadsides left out of the page because MSU says not to pick there); red and black raspberries typically ripen in July,

  strawberry yellow petals, fruit less juicy and less flavorful. GC-STR flowering "Apr.–June"; "Throughout much of the U.S. and s. Can."

### surv-land-ny-rules

- Guide years: HTG-GEN cover and footers (2026–2027; Sept. 1, 2026 to Aug. 31, 2027); FISHGUIDE cover ("Regulations in effect April 1,
  2026"). HuntFishNY app: HTG-PULL and DEC-FISHREG name it. No season dates or bag limits are given (spec 10 call 6); the frog and carp
  seasons and every species' dates are left to the guide.
- Licences table: Hunting: HTG-GEN pp. 10–11 (Hunter Education Certificate or previous hunting licence; "Minors under the age of 12
  may not obtain a hunting license or hunt wildlife"; "You must be at least 11 years of age to take this class"). Bowhunting privilege:
  HTG-GEN pp. 10–11 (hunting licence plus Bowhunter Education Certificate, NYS bowhunting stamp issued 1980 or later, or NYS junior
  bowhunting licence issued 1980 or later); HTG-BIG p. 23 (privilege required for bowhunting seasons). Muzzleloading privilege: HTG-GEN
  (current hunting licence); HTG-BIG p. 23. Turkey permit: HTG-GEN (required for all turkey hunters); HTG-TURKEY p. 50 ("You must carry
  your hunting license and turkey permit while you hunt."). Migratory birds: HTG-MIG pp. 53–54 (hunting licence; "must register
  annually with New York State's Harvest Information Program", proof carried; federal duck stamp "If you are 16 years or older and you
  hunt waterfowl", signed and carried). DMP: HTG-BIG p. 30 (one antlerless deer per permit, only in the WMU issued for). Trapping:
  HTG-GEN p. 11 ("Trapper Education Certificate or previous trapping license from any state or country"); marten permit HTG-FUR p. 61
  ("A free special permit is still required to trap marten in New York State."). Fishing: FISHGUIDE p. 89 (licence "while fishing or
  helping someone to fish", exceptions including "Persons under 16 years of age"); p. 90 free fishing days.
- Private land: HTG-GEN p. 12 ("does not give the holder any right to go on private property without permission of the landowner").
  Licence not transferable: HTG-FUR p. 62. Mandatory trapper education course: DEC-TRAP ("Trappers must complete a mandatory trapper
  education course").
- Kinds of season: HTG-BIG pp. 23, 27, 30, 37 (Early Antlerless, Early Bowhunting, Regular, Late Bowhunting, Muzzleloading, Youth
  Firearms; privileges per season); bear seasons HTG-BIG p. 38; turkey spring and fall HTG-TURKEY p. 51; small game by species HTG-SMALL
  pp. 46–49; permanent water only in mink, muskrat, otter or beaver season HTG-FUR p. 61; closed season for fish FISHGUIDE p. 69 ("A
  person may not fish for a species (including catch and release) during the closed season"; released immediately) and p. 4 ("not even
  catch and release"). Unprotected species: HTG-GEN pp. 16–17 (porcupine, red squirrel, woodchuck, chipmunk, English sparrow, starling,
  rock pigeon, monk parakeet; licence and legal implement still required).
- Hours: HTG-BIG p. 20 ("Big game hunting hours are 1/2-hour before sunrise to 1/2-hour after sunset (see page 80)."); HTG-SMALL pp.
  48–49 (cottontail, hare, squirrel, pheasant, bobwhite, ruffed grouse sunrise to sunset); HTG-TURKEY p. 51 (spring "1/2 hour before
  sunrise to noon"; the fall hours were garbled in the extracted text and are not given); HTG-MIG p. 54 ("All other migratory game birds
  may be taken from one-half hour before sunrise until sunset."; woodcock "from sunrise to sunset"). Sunday: HTG-BIG p. 20 ("Sunday
  hunting is allowed in all areas of New York State.").
- Always illegal: HTG-GEN pp. 16–17 (motor vehicle, vehicle lights, public road; unloaded long guns and crossbows in vehicles;
  automatic; silencer; semiautomatic over 6 rounds with exceptions; spear except frogs; explosive arrow; drug delivery device; "It is
  illegal to hunt with the aid of bait or over any baited area" for big game, upland game birds, turkey, waterfowl). HTG-BIG p. 20
  ("Intentional feeding or baiting of deer or bear is prohibited at all times of year."; "Take big game while the deer or bear is in
  water."; rimfire, under 20 gauge, multi-projectile, bows under 35 lb, barbed broadheads), p. 21 (dogs except leashed tracking dog
  licence; "Hunting bear with the aid of bait or dogs is prohibited."), p. 22 ("It is unlawful to sell deer or bear meat."). HTG-TURKEY
  p. 50 (no rifle or air gun; no bait; no electronic calling device during the open season; no dog in spring; no live decoys). HTG-MIG
  p. 55 (baiting, live decoys, recorded calls with exceptions, motorboat or sailboat unless motor off or sail furled and stopped, rifles;
  "No person shall kill or cripple any migratory game bird without making a reasonable effort" to retrieve it) and p. 54 ("Non-toxic shot
  is required for hunting any migratory game bird, except woodcock, everywhere in New York State."). HTG-SMALL p. 46 (native snakes,
  lizards, salamanders; turtles other than snapping turtles; spruce grouse).
- Distances: HTG-GEN p. 17 (500 ft firearm, 250 ft crossbow, 150 ft bow from school, playground, occupied factory or church; crossbow 500
  ft in Suffolk and Westchester; same from dwelling, farm building or occupied structure unless owner, lessee, immediate family,
  employee or consent; not over any part of a public highway). Blaze orange or pink: HTG-BIG p. 20 ("Any person hunting deer or bear
  with a firearm or a person who is accompanying someone hunting…"; 250 sq. in. solid visible from all directions, or 250 sq. in.
  patterned at least 50%, above the waist; or a hat at least 50% orange or pink).
- Tagging: HTG-BIG p. 22 ("Immediately fill in all information and sign the carcass tag"; "Report your harvest online, by phone, or
  HuntFishNY mobile app within 48 hours as required by law."), p. 21 (carcass tag once the animal leaves your possession; e-tag
  immediately); HTG-TURKEY p. 50 ("Users of paper tags must report within 48 hours of the harvest."); HTG-GEN p. 15 (reporting reduced
  "to 48 hours (no longer 7 days)"). Migratory birds: HTG-MIG p. 55 ("No person shall completely field dress any migratory game bird"
  before transport; head or one fully feathered wing attached). Pelt seal: HTG-FUR p. 62 (bobcat, fisher, otter, marten; seal before sale
  or transfer, mounting or tanning, leaving the state; "within 10 days after the close of the season in the WMU"; "Seals for these species
  cannot be sent through the mail."); HTG-PULL (possession tag and seal).
- Trap-check intervals (carried-in item): HTG-FUR p. 61, word for word: "In the Southern Zone: You must check traps once in each
  24-hour period."; "WMU 5C, 5F, 5G, 5H, 5J, 6F, 6J, and 6N: Visit once in each 48-hour period"; "WMU 5A, 6A, 6C, 6G, 6H, and 6K:" then
  "Traps set in water during the open season for beaver, otter, mink and muskrat: Visit once in each 48-hour period", "Body-gripping
  traps set on land: Visit once in each 48-hour period", "Restraining traps: Visit once in each 24-hour period". DEC-TRAPREG gives the
  same intervals ("Visited once in each 48-hour period", "Visited once in each 24-hour period"; Southern Zone wording identical). The two
  WMU lists together are the Northern Zone WMUs the guide lists for trap checking; no other Northern Zone WMU is named. "Restraining
  trap" definition: HTG-FUR p. 61 ("A device used to capture and restrain a mammal."). Neither source defines "visit" or "check".
  ECL § 11-1101 sets no interval. Year recorded: 2026–27 guide.
- Legal and illegal traps: HTG-FUR p. 61 ("Snares may not be used for trapping."; "Box or cage traps are legal for all species."; no
  cage trap designed to take more than one muskrat; "On land, foothold traps must be 5¾ inches or smaller (inside jaw spread)."; "Teeth
  are not allowed on foothold traps."; "Foothold traps larger than 4 inches set on land must have a pan tension device and be covered when
  set."; "During beaver or otter season, foothold traps up to 7¼ inches are allowed if set under water."; "A foothold trap larger than
  7¼ inches is never legal to use."; "Body-gripping traps more than 7½ inches may never be used on land."; Adirondack WMU bait or lure
  rule; name and address or DEC customer ID on all traps), p. 62 (closed beaver or otter season: water foothold no larger than 5¾ in.),
  p. 63 (Southern Zone beaver trigger rules over 8½ in.), p. 64 ("A body-gripping trap measuring less than 5½ inches may be set in any
  manner with or without the use of bait."; 5½ to 7½ in. limits on bait and set). DEC-TRAPREG agrees. ECL § 11-1101(5)(c) ("use, locate
  or set a snare or a device consisting of a noose of any material whereby an animal may be taken"), (7)(c) ("smoke, chemicals, gas or
  poison shall not be used on or near any trap" for listed furbearers), (4) ("any trap or deadfall").
- Deadfalls: looked for in HTG-FUR, DEC-TRAPREG, DEC-TRAP and ECL. None allows or forbids them by name; DEC-TRAPREG's definition of
  trapping includes "traps, deadfalls and other devices commonly used to take wildlife"; ECL (4) names "any trap or deadfall". The page
  says so and adds a labelled app caution (D190).
- Trap placement: HTG-FUR p. 62 ("within 100 feet of a house, school, playground, or church"; ECL (12): without "the written consent"
  of the owner or lessee; "You may not set a trap on a public road."; culvert or ditch unless posted or landowner forbids; 15 ft beaver
  dam, den or house with exceptions; "You may not set or stake a trap prior to 7:00 AM on opening day."; "No one may disturb a trap
  lawfully set by another person."; "No one may remove a lawfully trapped animal from another person's trap."; "You must attempt to
  release any animals that are accidentally captured when the season is closed"; "If the animal is injured to the extent you believe it
  will not survive, humanely dispatch it."; no legal provision to keep it without DEC permission; firearm on a trapped animal without a
  hunting licence from 16; junior trappers 12–15 need a hunting licence and an accompanying adult), p. 61 (5 ft muskrat house; no full
  suspension; carcass bait on foothold sets "shall be completely covered at the time the trap is set or visited", hidden from directly
  above), p. 64 (land body-gripping traps 100 ft from a public trail except on WMAs).
- Fishing: DEC-FISHGEN and FISHGUIDE pp. 68–72 (angling "taking fish by hook and line"; "no more than 3 lines with or without a rod";
  5 lures or baits, 15 hook points; "Anglers must be in immediate attendance when their lines are in the water."; "The use of set lines
  where the angler is not in immediate attendance is prohibited."; "No more than 7 ice-fishing lines in any combination of devices may be
  used, unless otherwise noted in Special Regulations."; ice-fishing line defined to include "hand line, tip-up, tip down"; 5 lures or
  baits, 15 hook points, immediate attendance; hand lines only May 1 to November 14; ice fishing permitted on most waters except where
  special regulations say and for waters in the nine named counties; shanties name and address in letters at least 3 inches, removed by
  March 15; nets: landing net, baitfish nets, one dip net for smelt, suckers, alewives, blueback herring; "No other use of nets to collect
  fish is permitted."; gaffs only ice fishing or bowfishing; frogs by spear, club, hook or hand with a hunting or fishing licence, gun or
  longbow needs a small game hunting licence; native salamanders and snakes not as bait). FISHGUIDE p. 79 (minnow trap "maximum entrance
  diameter 1"", maximum length 20"; seine or scap net up to 36 sq. ft), p. 78 (personally caught baitfish only in the same water; no
  overland transport by motor vehicle except in a designated corridor), p. 71 ("The taking of fish by spear or spear guns is prohibited at
  all times"; no spears in the Adirondack Park, on Lake George or within 200 ft of their high-water mark; "The taking of fish by snatching
  or blind snatching (page 69) is prohibited at all times"), p. 69 (snatching defined; snagging a type of snatching; daily limit and size).
  HTG-SMALL p. 46 ("A hunting license is required to take frogs with a gun, bow, or crossbow").
- Carp by bow, conflict: DEC-FISHGEN ("Carp may be taken by a longbow (recurve or compound) or crossbow in any number or size from May
  15-September 30"; "No other fish may be taken with a bow."). HTG-GEN p. 16 ("Crossbows may not be used to take carp or any other
  fish."). The more cautious is used: the page shows both and says, as the app's caution, to use a longbow (D191). Dates left out.
- Left out: the fall turkey hours (garbled), species seasons and bag limits, frog and snapping turtle seasons, the Northern Zone
  dog-and-rifle rule, firearm possession rules in deer season, DEC law enforcement phone line (no dial control), the smelt and sucker
  net waters and sizes beyond "as the guide gives", the "frightening fish out of concealment" rule (FISHGUIDE p. 59, a special
  regulation, not statewide).
- Looked for and not found: a trapper education age or course length (HTG-FUR, HTG-GEN give none beyond the certificate); a fishing-guide
  definition of "tip-up" (only inside "ice-fishing line"); explosives, poison or electricity for fish (not in DEC-FISHGEN or the parts of
  FISHGUIDE read); a statewide personal baitfish possession limit.

### surv-land-after-fallout

- Do first 1: surv-fallout-water-and-food "Food to leave alone", word for word: "No current source opened says when milk from your own
  animals, or wild game and fish, can be used after fallout. This app’s caution: treat them like food that was outdoors, and don’t use
  them until officials say you can." (copied from the file, curly apostrophes kept). Do first 2: the same section's list item, word for
  word: "Don’t pick or eat food from your garden until officials say you can (CDC, Ready.gov)." Do first 3 and 4: the app's own
  direction, resting on Do first 1 and 2 and on How long to stay in (when you may go out); no new rule.
- Read this first: CDC-FWM ("Do not pick or eat food from your garden until emergency officials determine it is safe to do so."; no
  milk, eggs, livestock, feed, game or fish); READY ("Do not consume food from your garden, or food or liquids that were outdoors and
  uncovered," / "until authorities tell you it is safe."; no milk, eggs, livestock, feed, game or fish). Jordan's v7.4 decision (radiation
  pack spec section 1): older federal civil defence publications fill the gap, named with year, dated, never "safe".
- Garden food: EPA-PAG section 4.6.1 p. 55 ("Protective actions might include restrictions on consumption of garden produce or locally
  produced foods."); section 4.6 p. 54 (food and feed guidance is FDA's). FDA-1998 p. 3 (scope: "accidents at nuclear power plants and
  many other types of accidents"; written for state and local agencies; no nuclear detonation), p. 16 (surface removal by "brushing,
  washing, or peeling"; "holding to allow for radioactive decay"; no home gardens or households mentioned). ITE-1968 chapter 2 ("Since
  radiation passing through food does not contaminate it, the only danger would be the actual swallowing of fallout particles" / "that
  happened to be on the food itself" / "(or on the can or package containing the food), and these could be wiped or washed off.").
  No source gives a wait time for garden food.
- Milk: surv-fallout-water-and-food's 1968 sentence quoted word for word (ITE-1968 chapter 2: "If cows graze on contaminated pasture and
  swallow fallout particles that contain some radioactive elements," / "their milk might be harmful to the thyroid glands of infants and
  small children."; "canned or powdered milk for a few weeks" if authorities say the supply is contaminated). FDA-1998 p. 17 ("removal of
  lactating dairy animals and meat animals from contaminated feeds and pasture"; "substitution of uncontaminated water for contaminated
  water"), p. 5 ("placing dairy cows on stored feed"). EPA-PAG footnote 41 p. 55 ("Liquid beverages as well as milk are covered under the
  FDA food PAG (FDA 1998)."). No goat-milk rule anywhere. Not shown: ITE-1968 "Milk contamination from fallout is not expected to be a
  serious problem after an attack." (it would loosen the checked caution; as v7.4 decided); FDA-1998 p. 5 "diversion of fresh milk to
  cheese or milk powder" (an agency-scale example; no household method) (D194).
- Animals: FDA-1998 p. 15 ("moving animals to shelter, corralling livestock"; "providing protected feed and water"), p. 17 (removal from
  contaminated feed and pasture; uncontaminated water). READY ("If you are instructed to stay inside during a radiation emergency, pets
  and service animals should be inside too." quoted). ITE-1968 Introduction ("Special advice for rural families on emergency actions
  related to crops and livestock" / "is available from the U.S. Department of Agriculture."); that advice was not looked up (D195).
  PNA-1985: no farm animals, feed, dairy animals, eggs, game, fish or garden produce (milk only as a household drink, pp. 25–27).
- Eggs: not in CDC-FWM, READY, EPA-PAG (parts read), FDA-1998 (protective actions; poultry only in import tables), ITE-1968, PNA-1985.
  App caution labelled (D193).
- Wild game, fish: not in CDC-FWM, READY, EPA-PAG (parts read), FDA-1998, ITE-1968 (fish only as canned shelf life), PNA-1985. The page
  says so plainly and repeats the checked rule.
- Not shown (would loosen the checked caution): ITE-1968 "Most of the Nation's remaining food supplies would be usable after an attack."
  and "Reaping, threshing, canning and other processing would prevent any dangerous quantities of fallout particles" / "from getting into
  processed foods." (about the national food supply); EPA-PAG p. 22 (grain products and canned milk and vegetables stored for weeks to
  months "will not present a risk from radioiodine": an official-planning statement about stored commercial food, which belongs to
  surv-fallout-water-and-food) (D194).
- "Safe" appears only in CDC-FWM's page title in the source line (v7.4 ruling 24).

### Butchering deer and small game (new)

- Before you start: Indiana DNR tools ("A sharp, short knife", "A sharp fillet or boning knife", bone saw, gambrel, "A cool workspace");
  NMSU CR508 ("a meat saw or fine-toothed carpenter's saw, a sharp narrow-bladed knife"); NYS DOH gloves, no eating/drinking/smoking,
  "Butchering tools should never be used for any other purpose", "Keep butchering tools separate from utensils regularly used in the
  kitchen", "Avoid handling or cutting through the skull or spinal cord"; CWHL "Take your time, do one animal at a time!", "Store each
  deer's meat in its own labeled container", "Debone that deer! Keep contact with the brain, spinal cord, lymph nodes, and spleen to a
  minimum", "Avoid sawing into bone where possible", trim generously near shattered bone, spine, skull; NDSU FN536 "Bone out carcasses".
- Hanging and skinning, step order: (1) Mass notes "hanging on a gambrel by its hind legs with the head facing the ground"; NMSU CR507
  "Hang the carcass from the hind legs for skinning"; Indiana DNR at least 8 feet off the ground (8 ft = 2.4 m). (2) NMSU CR507 cut
  around hock and knee, down the inside of each leg. (3) Indiana DNR "Remove the front legs at the joint. Take your knife and cut a circle
  down to the bone around the joint."; Mass split front-leg skin on the hair seam. (4) NMSU CR507 pull with both hands, cut flesh back,
  abdomen last. (5) Mass: work down the neck; "At the base of the head, cut through the top of the spinal column with a knife or bone
  saw" (paraphrased); NYS DOH wash if brain/spinal tissue handled. (6) Indiana DNR "Wash any hair off the meat with cold water." Gutless
  alternative: Kentucky Afield steps 1 to 31 (on its side, hide along the spine, shoulder, hindquarter, tenderloin, backstrap, neck,
  flip; game bags or pillow cases in the shade; thermometer on the ice "below 40 degrees").
- Quartering order: Penn State video (shoulders, backstraps, tenderloins, hind legs) and Mass notes (shoulders "there is no joint or bone
  structure to break through", neck, tenderloins, backstraps, hind quarters); Kentucky backstrap ½-inch cut, cross cut, tease off;
  tenderloin "Grab the tubular muscle running along the inside of the spine"; NMSU tenderloin "near the pelvic area"; flank and rib meat
  (Kentucky, Penn State video); Mass rib meat "If in good condition with no gut material"; hind leg: Penn State video ball joint "Stay
  tight to the hipbones", Kentucky "sever the joint by cutting directly into it", NMSU "cut through it with a knife rather than a saw to
  avoid bone dust and marrow"; Indiana DNR second person. Disposal: Mass "Bones, sinew, and hide: Bag for disposal"; HPAI sheet (pets).
- Boning out the hind leg: Indiana DNR knee joint leaves the shank; femur out; "the sirloin, which is round and hugs the front of the
  femur", top round, bottom round, eye of round; Mass "Sirloin tip (round tip, 'football roast')", waxy gland "Do not grind it"; NMSU
  meat near the long tendon "too tough for steak"; Penn State video and NMSU natural seams, each muscle in its own connective tissue.
- Cuts table (every cell): backstrap steaks "usually 3/4 inch thick" (NMSU), roasts and ends for stew (Penn State video); tenderloin
  thick or thin, butterflied (NMSU); sirloin tip roast or thin steak 1/4 to 3/8 inch (NMSU), large braised roast (Mass); rounds thin
  steaks cut just before frying or roasts (NMSU), jerky, braising (Mass; Mass also lists corning, not carried: see Keeping game meat);
  shoulder arm roast, small thin steaks (NMSU), braised blade roast or ground (Mass), stew, grind, sausage (Penn State video; "sausage"
  not carried, see the sausage warn); neck mincemeat, stew, grind or roast whole (NMSU), roasts (Kentucky); ribs plates for barbecue or
  stew (NMSU), grilling or grinding (Kentucky), rib meat to the grind (Mass); brisket barbeque (Kentucky); shank trimmed for grinding
  (NMSU); flank jerky, plate steaks, grinding (Kentucky); trimmings grind, stew, jerky (NMSU), grind (Indiana). Conversions (app's own):
  3/4 in = 2 cm, 1/4 to 3/8 in = 6 to 10 mm. "Where it comes from" cells: Kentucky (backstrap, tenderloin, brisket, flank), Indiana
  (sirloin, shank), NMSU and Mass (rounds, shoulder, neck, ribs); "Mincemeat" not carried.
- Trimming: NCHFP jerky "Trim and discard all fat from meat because it becomes rancid quickly"; Indiana DNR fat "has a bitter taste";
  NDSU FN536 "The distinctive flavor of game meats is mainly due to the fat they contain"; Indiana silver skin; Mass silver skin and
  tendons; NYS DOH "Lymph nodes can be eliminated by boning out the meat and carefully trimming the fat and connective tissue"; CWHL lymph
  nodes between muscles; Penn State "Remove all visible dirt, feces, hair, and bloodshot areas"; NYS DOH bruised or discolored meat, all
  bullets and fragments, generous distance from the wound channel, "Discard meat with excessive bullet damage"; lead warn from NYS DOH
  ("too small to detect by sight, feel, or even when eating"; "Ground meat from lead-shot game tends to contain more lead fragments than
  whole muscle cuts"; children and people who can get pregnant). Not carried: NMSU's soak of bloodshot meat in salt water (NYS DOH says
  discard bruised meat; the more cautious used).
- Heart, liver, tongue: NM Game and Fish heart ("best eaten fresh. You can refrigerate it for up to a couple of days"; cold water while
  pumping; "cut away and discard all fat, arteries, veins and blood vessels"; "Discard any parts of the heart damaged by the bullet or
  broadhead"); liver "off colored, with cysts, or in otherwise poor condition" discard; soak 24 hours, water changed every eight hours;
  slices ½ inch (13 mm). Michigan DNR flukes. FM 21-76 p. 98 "Cut the tongue out, skin it, boil it until tender, and eat it." NYS DOH
  "Avoid handling the brain and spinal tissues or fluids, saliva and mouth parts", tonsils among the parts that "may have abnormal
  infectious proteins called CWD prions", "Other organs (liver, kidney, heart and salivary glands) may also pose a risk". Tongue: app's
  caution (D164).
- Never eat: NYS DOH prion list (brain, spinal cord and other nervous tissue, spleen, pancreas, eyes, tonsils, lymph nodes), "Discard
  intestines"; DEC high-risk parts; FM 21-76 p. 98 "You can also cook and eat the brain" (reported, not followed); Penn State venison
  organs; MDC rabbit.
- Bones and fat: NMSU CR508 backbone "sections for soup stock"; NYS DOH and CWHL as above. Looked for and not found: a source for stock
  from other deer bones, and for rendering deer fat (D165).
- Grinding: NMSU and Indiana (trimmings, shank, neck, flank); CWHL "remove fat and other tissues before grinding meat"; NYS DOH "If you
  prepare your own ground meat, thoroughly clean and disinfect all equipment after use"; Penn State "Thoroughly clean and sanitize all
  equipment, including the tabletop meat grinder"; Mass "Never put your hand near or in the grinder's throat". Looked for and not found:
  grinding without power (Mass says only that electric grinders reduce work compared with hand grinders; no method).
- Sausage warn: NCHFP section 5.1.1 nitrates/nitrites "inhibit Clostridium botulinum"; 6.2.3 "Mistakenly using sodium nitrite instead of
  NaCl in typical curing recipes can lead to a lethal dose"; 5.2.4 E. coli O157:H7 "can survive the typical dry fermentation processing
  conditions"; 6.7 "We do not recommend preparing homemade, non-fermented sausages that are not fully cooked"; CDC trichinellosis curing.
- Small game and birds: MDC rabbit "Separate the front and hind quarters from the carcass at the 'shoulder' and 'hip' joints"; MDC
  squirrel "Make sure the carcass is free of hair", "wash the body cavity"; Penn State birds "Separate the carcass by pulling the breast
  apart from the neck, back, and legs", bloodshot areas, 165°F; Clemson ducks wings at the joints, head, pinfeathers, "scalding the birds
  in hot water (145 °F)" (63°C, app's conversion), upland birds soaked "in cold water for one to two hours"; NYS DOH shot and feathers.
- Knives and clean work: Penn State and NDSU whetstone or steel; Mass dull blade "over exertion which could lead to a potential injury",
  wash and sharpen afterwards; NDSU and Penn State warm soapy water; CWHL "Wash knives and tools with soap and hot water between
  animals"; NYS DOH wash, then "Rinse tools and work surfaces with either boiling water (212°F) or sanitize with a bleach solution or
  chemical sanitizer"; NYS DOH CWD soak: "Soak cleaned knives and tools for one hour in a fresh solution of household chlorine bleach
  (unscented) mixed with an equal amount of water (for example, 1-quart bleach with 1-quart water), air dry, then rinse with clean water";
  "Wipe down cleaned counters and other surfaces with the bleach solution and allow them to air dry" (CWHL gives the same 50% mix). 1 quart
  = 0.95 L (app's conversion). The never-drink and never-mix lines follow the bleach rule of the land spec (section 7) and Clean and
  disinfect's checked warns.
- Wrapping: Penn State meal-size portions "about one pound", wrap tightly, remove air, label and date; NMSU keep chunks whole, cut steaks
  just before cooking. 1 lb = 0.45 kg.

Conflicts: Mass removes the head through the spinal column, NYS DOH says avoid cutting through the spinal cord: both shown, NYS DOH's
precautions added (D169). NMSU backbone stock against NYS DOH and CWHL (D165). FM 21-76 eats brain and tongue against NYS DOH (D164).

### Keeping game meat (new)

- Cold and time table: Minnesota DOH "deer 3 to 5 6 to 12", "rabbit 1 to 2 12", "duck, goose 1 to 2 6" (days at 40°F, months at 0°F);
  USU "Fresh cuts: Refrigerate for 1 to 2 days" (used, shorter); FoodSafety.gov ground meats "1 to 2 days" and "3 to 4 months", soups and
  stews with meat "3 to 4 days" and "2 to 3 months", "The guidelines for freezer storage are for quality only", "frozen foods stored
  continuously at 0°F (-18°C) or below can be kept indefinitely"; Clemson birds "used within three days", frozen "within six months".
  Also seen and not used in the table: Penn State 2 to 3 days fridge and 9 to 12 months frozen; NDSU FN536 2 to 3 days and "three to four
  months in the freezer"; USU roasts frozen 1 year, ground 6 to 9 months; NDSU FN155 most wild game up to one year frozen. NDSU FN536 "Freeze
  only the amount that will become solidly frozen within 24 hours"; Penn State "do not refreeze thawed products".
- Hanging: NYS DOH 45°F (above); Penn State "hold the carcass at 40°F(4°C) or below for two to three days, at most"; Cornell 4-H guide
  "Keep the deer below 40°F during aging", "hung by its hind feet with the skin on", "it is not necessary to age the meat to achieve
  tender results"; NDSU FN536 "34 to 37 F for 10 to 14 days", "Aging is not recommended for carcasses with little or no fat covering",
  "Two to three days is sufficient", not needed for sausage meat; NMSU CR507 "If temperatures stay at or around 32 °F, then venison can be
  aged for as long as 10 to 12 days"; USU 34 to 36°F (not carried); Kentucky thermometer on the ice; NMSU quarter and ice.
- Winter cold as the freezer: FM 21-76 p. 99 "In cold climates, you can freeze and keep meat indefinitely." "Freezing is not a means of
  preparing meat." "You must still cook it before eating."; FoodSafety.gov continuously at 0°F; Preserving food's NYS DOH sentence, quoted
  word for word; Penn State refreeze; NDSU FN536 carcass freezing toughens. Risk sentence labelled as the app's caution (D163).
- Jerky (NCHFP jerky page): "If pork or wild game is used to make jerky, the meat should be treated to kill the trichinella parasite";
  "freeze a portion that is 6 inches or less thick at 0ºF or below for at least 30 days"; gut contents: "It is best to avoid making jerky
  from this meat and use it only in ways that it will be thoroughly cooked"; "Partially freeze meat to make slicing easier"; "Slice meat
  no thicker than ¼ inch"; "Trim and discard all fat"; "Cover and refrigerate 1-2 hours or overnight"; "bring strips and marinade to a
  boil and boil for 5 minutes before draining and drying"; "If strips are more than ¼ inch thick, the length of time may need to be
  increased"; "check the temperature of several strips with a metal stem-type thermometer"; "dehydrator or oven preheated to 140ºF";
  "Begin checking samples after 3 hours"; "cracks but does not break when it is bent"; "Properly dried jerky will keep at room temperature
  two weeks in a sealed container"; "refrigerate or freeze jerky"; "glass jars or heavy plastic food storage bags"; "Raw poultry is
  generally not recommended for use in making jerky". NCHFP review 6.4 "Wild game (bear, elk, etc.) must be treated to destroy
  Trichinella by heating to 170°F, since some strains of Trichinella are freeze resistant (CDC 1985)"; 5.4.6 "USDA recommends attaining an
  internal temperature of at least 170°F"; 5.4.6 "Several outbreaks of E. coli O157:H7 have occurred in venison jerky". UAF "Heat meat in
  marinade to 160°F. Heat to boiling (212°F) for game meat."; "To be safe, do not use bear meat for jerky." Penn State jerky "one to two
  months under refrigeration (< 40°F [4°C])". USDA dehydrator sentence quoted from Preserving food. CDC "Freezing wild game meats may not
  effectively kill all worms". Conversions (app's own): 170°F = 77°C (76.7), 212°F = 100°C, 140°F = 60°C, 6 in = 15 cm, 1/4 in = 6 mm.
- Smoking: NDSU FN155 smoked deer jerky ("Pump with brine (two pounds commercial saltcure mixture per gallon of water)"; crock or
  USDA-approved plastic, "Do not use plastic containers such as garbage cans, plastic bags or supermarket ice cream buckets"; submerged;
  "Store in cooler (38 F) for 10 days"; "Every two days, change the position of the meat"; "smoke five hours at 150 F"; "Hang to dry at
  room temperature (about two weeks)"); NDSU hardwoods, "Never use a soft wood such as pine". FM 21-76 p. 98 ("The intent is to produce
  smoke, not heat"; "Do not use resinous wood"; "no more than 6 centimeters thick"; "Meat smoked overnight in this manner will last about
  1 week"; "Two days of continuous smoking will preserve the meat for 2 to 4 weeks"; "dark, curled, brittle stick and you can eat it
  without further cooking"). NCHFP 6.3 "Smoke itself, without proper cooking, is not an effective food preservative", "Caution should be
  used when smoking meats at temperatures in the danger zone 40-140°F for prolonged periods of time", "meats must have been salted or cured
  first"; 6.1.3 "The danger zone for microbial growth is 40-140°F"; 6.8 storage refrigerated or frozen. CO: Carbon monoxide's summary
  quoted word for word. Conversions: 38°F = 3°C, 150°F = 66°C, 2 lb = 0.9 kg, 1 gal = 3.8 L.
- Sun and air drying: FM 21-76 p. 99 (strips about 6 mm, with the grain; "sunny location with good air flow"; "out of the reach of
  animals and cover them to keep blowflies off"; "Allow the meat to dry thoroughly before eating"; "dry, crisp texture and will not feel
  cool to the touch"). USDA sun-drying sentence quoted from Preserving food. NCHFP Sun Drying "Vegetables (with the exception of vine dried
  beans) and meats are not recommended for out-of-doors drying."
- Salting and brining: FM 21-76 p. 99 ("soaking it thoroughly in a saltwater solution"; "The solution must cover the meat"; "Wash off the
  salt before cooking"; no strength or time given). NDSU FN155 corning: "3 lb salt", "10 oz sugar", "2 ounces sodium nitrate", "½ ounce
  sodium nitrite" (amounts not carried, D166), spices, six gallons; "The ideal temperature for corning meat is about 38 F"; one third more
  salt per 15 F above 38 F, "At 83 F" six pounds total; 15 days, stir and rotate on days 5 and 10; boil, skim, simmer "for about five hours
  or until tender"; "cooked and consumed within one week or frozen for up to one month"; its sweet pickle cure "Add commercial cure to
  pickle solution according to package directions" and "If temperature becomes warm and brine becomes ropy, remove meat". NCHFP 6.2.2
  "Only food grade salt without additives, e.g., iodine"; 6.2.3 commercial mixes, lethal dose; 6.2.4 "Curing should be carried out at a
  temperature between 35°F and 40°F", "the upper temperature is set to limit microbial growth"; 5.2.1 "C. botulinum thrives in moist foods
  that are low in salt (less than 10%)". Conversions: 6 gal = 23 L, 3 lb = 1.4 kg, 10 oz = 280 g, 15°F difference = 8°C, 83°F = 28°C,
  6 lb = 2.7 kg.
- Left out: NDSU FN155 dry cure ("6 pounds salt", "3 pounds sugar", nitrate or nitrite, "at 38 F for two days per pound of leg, or
  approximately four to six weeks") and sweet pickle cure (three days per pound at 38°F); pemmican (no source opened).

Conflicts:
- Jerky trichinella step: NCHFP's jerky page freezes wild game 30 days; Cornell 4-H preserving guide freezes game at 5°F for 20 days; UAF
  freezes 1 to 2 months; CDC and NCHFP's own review say some strains are freeze resistant. The heat step (170°F) is the one the page
  relies on (D162). Cornell 4-H preserving guide's 160°F after boiling not used for game (below 165°F).
- Jerky game temperature: NCHFP review 170°F; UAF boiling (212°F); USDA 160°F (meat). The page gives the NCHFP figure as the minimum and
  names UAF's boiling (closes D149 as logged in D162).
- Fridge time for deer cuts: USU 1 to 2 days; Penn State and NDSU 2 to 3; Minnesota DOH 3 to 5. Shortest used (D161).
- Hanging: NYS DOH below 45°F for several days; Penn State 40°F, 2 to 3 days at most; NDSU 10 to 14 days at 34 to 37°F; NMSU 10 to 12
  days near 32°F. Penn State used (D160).
